body.text: In short:
In 2023 the ABC hired a freelancer to provide video from Gaza.
Roshdi Al Sarraj was killed by an Israeli air strike early in the war, and years later his death was listed on an Israeli military website as a Hamas operative.
Despite multiple questions over several weeks, Israel's military has refused the ABC's requests for evidence.
Israel's military has ignored or declined to answer the ABC's multiple requests for evidence a Palestinian journalist it engaged as a freelancer in Gaza was a Hamas operative.
It comes after reports in The Australian newspaper that the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) had evidence the man held a role in Hamas's military wing as observer and deputy squad commander.
Roshdi Al Sarraj was killed by an Israeli air strike on October 22, 2023, two weeks after Hamas' deadly attacks on Israel triggered the war in Gaza.
Al Sarraj was engaged by the ABC in 2023 in the very early stages of the war to provide video for its 7.30 program.
Since the war began, Israel has controlled all access to the Gaza Strip — and blocked international media from accessing and reporting independently there.
The ABC has repeatedly requested access and has only been allowed in for two very limited periods.
The first was in August 2025 when the ABC travelled to the Kerem Shalom aid depot in the far south of the strip, away from fighting and populated areas.
The second was in October that same year when the ABC was taken to the edge of Gaza City weeks after the ceasefire was announced.
These were embeds, where journalists are taken into areas under the strict supervision of the IDF and do not interact with locals.
In October 2026, the IDF included Al Sarraj in its publication of The Press Files — a website listing 170 Palestinians killed in the war who it claimed were terrorists masquerading as journalists.
The level of detail attached to each name varied.

Some included photos of the journalists carrying out their work alongside photos of them in military outfits brandishing weapons, or appearing on posters designed by the terrorist organisations they worked for labelling them as martyrs for the cause.

Others included details such as military ID numbers and documents the IDF said it discovered during raids of Hamas command centres showing service records — both the originals in Arabic and seemingly machine-translated versions in English.
The IDF said the people in the list had been lauded as slain journalists when they should actually be condemned as terrorists.
It listed Al Sarraj as a member of Hamas.
However, the evidence provided in many cases has been scant and not conclusive of a terrorist affiliation.
Al Sarraj is the only person on the list the IDF said had worked for the ABC.
From October to November 20, there was only a grainy photo of the man wearing a flak jacket labelled "press".

In the original publication, an ID number was also listed, but this was not a military identifier, rather a Palestinian ID number the likes of which are given to every Palestinian in Gaza and the West Bank under a system which Israel has oversight of.
Liberal senator Sarah Henderson recently corrected the parliamentary record over this distinction, after mistakenly asserting that the IDF had Al Sarraj's military ID.
The Press Files listed Al Sarraj as an operative in Hamas' military wing, based on multiple intelligence sources, but has, until now, not publicly cited what the sources are.
Following the publication of The Press Files, the ABC made repeated requests for further information from the IDF about the sources.
No evidence was provided and the ABC's approaches went largely ignored.
On November 20, The Australian newspaper reported on a document which the IDF said showed Al Sarraj was a Hamas operative.

Screenshots of the heavily redacted document published by the paper purport to show Al Sarraj's military ID number as well as note that he joined Hamas as a foot soldier in 2011 when he was 19 and was promoted in 2018 at the age of 26.
The IDF told the paper it discovered the document in November 2023, just weeks after Al Sarraj was killed.
Following this reporting, the ABC has again made multiple requests for a copy of the document but has not yet received a response.
The document relied on by The Australian has since been made available on the IDF's The Press Files website, along with other details on Al Sarraj's profile.
The IDF did not reply directly to the ABC but posted the screenshot of the document on social media platform X.
There are no identifying markers on the document to suggest where it is from or what the list is for, and every line has been blurred other than that which includes Al Sarraj's name.
The Committee to Protect Journalists, an independent non-profit organisation which investigates cases of killed journalists, has maintained Al Sarraj was a civilian journalist.
In a statement to the ABC, the CPJ said its September 2026 investigation into Al Sarraj "did not identify any evidence" he was a combatant.
"Our rigorous investigation required CPJ researchers to interview at least two new credible independent sources on each individual, in addition to in-depth, desk-based research," the statement said.
What did the ABC do to verify this claim with the IDF?
On Saturday, October 3,the ABC first asked the IDF's International Press Desk about its listing of Al Sarraj as a Hamas militant, including requesting evidence of the allegation.
The usual approach is to message the press team via WhatsApp.
One day later, the IDF requested an extension in time to provide a response. Then it stopped responding altogether.
The ABC made three follow-up requests on October 5 and 6, but no response was provided and correspondence was ignored by the IDF.
On October 6, a request for comment on a separate story was immediately acknowledged, and a response to that story was provided a week later.
The ABC again followed up its questions about Al Sarraj and the military press team claimed it had been experiencing "internet issues" and was "looking into getting an answer".

When pressed on when a response would be provided, and why previous messages had been read and ignored, the IDF said it understood the "frustration" but insisted giving "the best answer possible" can take time.
What did the IDF tell the ABC?
The IDF eventually responded on Wednesday, October 14, just under two weeks after the initial query.
The IDF told the ABC it had thoroughly reviewed the information and published it alongside the sources that could be disclosed:
"In the case of the journalist in question, the information available to the IDF unequivocally indicates his affiliation with the Islamic Jihad.
"The IDF bases its assessments on information collected and examined by professional authorities, including the cross-referencing of information from multiple sources.
"The information published regarding the journalists is based on reliable findings indicating their affiliation with terrorist organizations and their involvement in activities on their behalf."
The reference to Palestinian Islamic Jihad did not match The Press Files's listing of Al Sarraj as a member of Hamas.
When the ABC sought to clarify this, the IDF's message in the chat to the ABC was quickly edited to say "Hamas".
A further message asking for evidence to back up the IDF's assertion was read and ignored.
When the ABC became aware of The Australian's latest reporting, prior to its article being published, the broadcaster again requested the material.
The IDF has yet to respond to the ABC's latest questions but has posted a statement criticising the ABC on X.
